title: US civil rights: Brown, Montgomery and Little Rock (1954–1959)
summary: Segregation and its legal challenge, the Montgomery bus boycott, massive resistance in the South and federal intervention at Little Rock.

keyterms.definition: State and local laws in the US South enforcing racial segregation in schools, transport, housing and public facilities.
1896 Supreme Court ruling that segregation was constitutional if facilities were 'separate but equal'.
1954 Supreme Court ruling that segregated public schools were 'inherently unequal' and unconstitutional, overturning Plessy in education.
National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (1909); its legal team, led by Thurgood Marshall, fought segregation through the courts.
Organised white Southern opposition to desegregation, including the Southern Manifesto, school closures and White Citizens' Councils.
381-day boycott of Montgomery's buses (1955–56) by Black residents after Rosa Parks' arrest; it ended with bus desegregation.
Organisation formed in December 1955 to run the bus boycott, with Martin Luther King Jr as president.
Southern Christian Leadership Conference, founded in 1957 by King and other Black ministers to coordinate non-violent protest.
Nine Black students who integrated Central High School, Little Rock, Arkansas, in 1957 under federal troop protection.
First federal civil rights law since Reconstruction; created a Civil Rights Commission and a Justice Department civil rights division but did little to secure votes.
Peaceful protest such as boycotts, marches and sit-ins designed to expose injustice and force change, influenced by Gandhi and Christian teaching.

questions.text: The 1896 case ___ v. Ferguson established the 'separate but equal' doctrine.
questions.explanation: Plessy gave legal cover to Jim Crow segregation for nearly 60 years.

questions.prompt: Who led the NAACP's legal team in Brown v. Board of Education?
questions.explanation: Marshall argued the case; he later became the first Black Supreme Court justice (1967). Earl Warren was the Chief Justice who wrote the ruling.

questions.statement: The Brown ruling of May 1954 was unanimous.
questions.explanation: Chief Justice Earl Warren worked to secure a 9–0 decision so the ruling would carry maximum authority.

questions.prompt: What was the weakness of the 1955 'Brown II' ruling?
options: It ordered desegregation 'with all deliberate speed', allowing delay
questions.explanation: The vague timetable let Southern states delay; by 1964 only a tiny fraction of Black children in the Deep South attended integrated schools.

questions.prompt: Match each example to the form of massive resistance.

pairs.right: Closed public schools rather than integrate

questions.explanation: Resistance ranged from 'respectable' political opposition to terror.

questions.prompt: Why did the murder of Emmett Till in 1955 matter to the civil rights movement?
options: His killers were convicted, proving the system worked
His mother's open-casket funeral and the acquittal of his killers shocked and mobilised many
It led directly to the Brown ruling
It ended lynching in the South
questions.explanation: The 14-year-old's murder in Mississippi and the all-white jury's acquittal exposed Southern injustice nationwide.

questions.prompt: Put these events in chronological order.

questions.statement: President Eisenhower publicly campaigned for rapid school desegregation after Brown.
questions.explanation: Eisenhower was reluctant to endorse Brown, believing laws could not change hearts; he acted at Little Rock to uphold federal authority.

questions.text: The NAACP strategy was mainly to challenge segregation through the ___.
questions.explanation: Litigation produced landmark rulings but depended on enforcement, which is why direct action grew in importance.

questions.prompt: Which Supreme Court justice wrote the Brown decision?
questions.explanation: Warren, appointed by Eisenhower in 1953, led a court that became known for expanding civil rights.

questions.prompt: What triggered the Montgomery bus boycott?
options: The arrest of Rosa Parks on 1 December 1955
questions.explanation: Parks, an NAACP secretary, refused to give up her seat. The Women's Political Council, led by Jo Ann Robinson, quickly called a boycott.

questions.statement: Rosa Parks was a long-standing activist rather than simply a tired woman who acted on impulse.
questions.explanation: She had worked for the NAACP for over a decade and had attended training at the Highlander Folk School.

questions.text: Martin Luther King Jr became president of the Montgomery ___ Association.
questions.explanation: The MIA organised car pools and kept the boycott going for 381 days.

questions.prompt: What legally ended segregation on Montgomery's buses?
options: The federal case Browder v. Gayle, upheld by the Supreme Court in 1956
questions.explanation: The boycott's economic pressure mattered, but the court ruling forced integration in December 1956, showing how direct action and litigation worked together.

questions.prompt: Match each person to their role.

pairs.right: Women's Political Council leader who spread boycott leaflets
Local NAACP leader who bailed out Parks
NAACP leader who supported the Little Rock Nine

questions.explanation: Local leaders, many of them women, were vital to the movement's grassroots success.

questions.prompt: How did President Eisenhower respond to the Little Rock crisis in September 1957?
options: He sent the 101st Airborne Division and federalised the Arkansas National Guard
He asked the UN to mediate
questions.explanation: Eisenhower acted to enforce federal court orders and uphold federal authority, not out of enthusiasm for integration.

questions.prompt: Put these events in chronological order.
questions.explanation: December 1955, December 1956, early 1957, September 1957.

questions.text: In 1957 King and other ministers founded the ___ to coordinate protest across the South.
questions.explanation: The Southern Christian Leadership Conference based its work in Black churches.

questions.statement: The Civil Rights Act of 1957 quickly doubled the number of Black voters in the South.
questions.explanation: It was weakened in the Senate (Strom Thurmond made a record filibuster) and had little immediate effect on voter registration.

questions.prompt: What was the main significance of the Montgomery bus boycott?
options: It ended segregation across the South
It showed mass non-violent action could work and made King a national figure
It led to the Brown ruling
It was organised by the federal government
questions.explanation: Montgomery provided a model of disciplined community protest and brought King to national prominence.
